questions.q: What is the purpose of running nccl-tests (e.g., all_reduce_perf) when diagnosing a slow training job?
options: It replaces the need for NCCL in production training
It benchmarks raw collective performance in isolation from the training job, to establish what the fabric is actually capable of
It automatically fixes any InfiniBand cabling problems
It only measures GPU compute performance, not networking
questions.explain: nccl-tests exercises the same collectives NCCL uses during training, but as a standalone benchmark — letting you isolate whether a performance problem is in the fabric itself, independent of anything the training code is doing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say busbw (bus bandwidth) is more trustworthy than algbw (algorithm bandwidth) when comparing against a fabric's rated hardware bandwidth?
options: algbw is always higher than busbw, so it's more conservative
busbw accounts for the fact that a collective moves more bytes across the wire than the logical message size, via the 2(N-1)/N factor
busbw only measures CPU performance, not network performance
algbw and busbw are always identical, so it doesn't matter which is used
questions.explain: algbw is simply message size divided by time, which understates actual wire traffic. busbw multiplies algbw by the ring AllReduce factor 2(N-1)/N to reflect the real data movement, making it the correct number to compare against rated hardware bandwidth.

questions.q: If `ibstat` shows an InfiniBand link negotiated at a lower speed than its rated 400 Gb/s, what does this most likely indicate?
options: The training job's batch size is too large
A likely hardware or cabling problem on that specific link
NCCL_DEBUG was not set to INFO
The GPU driver needs to be reinstalled
questions.explain: A link stuck below its rated speed is a hardware-layer symptom (bad cable, degraded transceiver, etc.), not something addressed by training code or NCCL configuration — it's exactly the kind of problem ibstat and perfquery are meant to surface.

questions.q: During a training step, GPU compute utilization drops to near zero during the AllGather/ReduceScatter phase, and the step is slower than expected. What does this indicate?
options: The job is compute-bound, and more GPUs would help
The job is network-bound — the GPUs are idle waiting for data to arrive over the network
The checkpoint is corrupted
The model has too many parameters
questions.explain: If GPU utilization drops near zero specifically during the collective communication phases while the step remains slow, that's a strong signal the GPUs are sitting idle waiting on network transfers — a network-bound bottleneck rather than a compute-bound one.

questions.q: What is the recommended first step in this lesson's diagnostic checklist when a training job underperforms the capacity-planning estimate?
options: Immediately reduce the model's parameter count
Benchmark the fabric directly and in isolation using nccl-tests, before suspecting the training job itself
Switch from InfiniBand to Ethernet
Restart the Kubernetes cluster
questions.explain: The lesson's checklist starts with isolating the fabric's raw performance using nccl-tests, so you know what the hardware is actually capable of before trying to diagnose anything in the training code or job configuration itself.
